en: No beast could match his walk,
And no wind could match his gallop,
His four legs moving swiftly,
Whenever he simply set off,
The tips of the grass whispered.
When he trod upon black stone,
It scattered like millet;
A great bustard, large as a house,
Shrieked above his head.
They traveled without sparing their horses,
Going far, no little distance.
Crossing rugged ground,
Passing over mountain passes and stones.
The sight made the heart divide;
Ask not how the gray wolf fared—
He loomed like Opol-Too.
He rode Buurul, making him surge;
Buurul, restored to full flesh,
He mastered and made leap.
The sight made the heart divide;
His beauty appeared mountain-like.
Crossing a pass no phantom roamed,
Treading land no man reached,
The thoroughbred Bakai led the road;
How could the warriors hold back?
They reached Buurul-Tün.
There lay Buurul-Tün,
Its rugged hills in view,
Making a man's heart divide.
It was a land lying free,
Called Buurul-Ata.
No man traveled there;
Its beasts and creatures
Made any beholder marvel.
Its saplings were like plane trees,
Its birds like snowcocks;
God had truly created
And placed them there.
Its lizards were like snakes,
And its snakes were of every kind;
God Most High in his power
Created living creatures of every kind!
It was a land lying free;
Every beast and creature was there.
A cold wind roared from the valley,
Its breeze fragrant with violets;
Its grasses grew in separate kinds,
Fescue and dark sedge,
Gleaming when the wind blew,
Divided into countless varieties.
It had trees and branches;
Everything the ear had heard of
And the eye had seen was there!
On the plain on this side,
Its tortoises were as large as bowls.
It was a land lying free—
Would the Kyrgyz not settle there!
Would Argyn and Kyrgyz turn away,
As though it were a land unfit to camp?
Koumiss by day and girls by night—
Could such things fail to be there!
Wearing paired sable caps,
Could it be a place not to sing,
Drink koumiss, and court girls—
Could it be a place not to rejoice!
Could it be a place that could not contain
Wonders, festivities, and delights,
Where men could not revel in games,
Could they not set up an ordo here
And make it their abode!
It had hills and passes,
And countless varied highlands;
Projecting headlands came into view,
And looking on them divided the heart.
The finest things in the world
Appeared as visions before the eyes.
There lay Buurul-Tün;
Looking across its low hills,
There were bull-like and camel-like deer—
What wonders there were to see!
Long ago he had seen it thoroughly,
Lion Bakai, the mighty one.
He had seen wonders and lands,
And had seen many things alike.
Traveling a winding road,
Crossing land that curved around,
To the foot of Teshik-Tash,
My uncle, elder Bakai,
Now entered at speed
The edge of the Kara-Kum.
He crossed Buurul-Tün,
And now scattered the Kara-Kum.
He came to a ridge like a saddle back,
And had only just bent forward and crossed it;
On the far side, through the haze,
The Chinese call it Tyngsha—
He crossed that Tyngsha.
The tulpars beneath them,
If one spoke of their legs, were like clouds;
The ground beneath their tread burst apart,
And when they merely opened their mouths,
The earth split with a crash.
Their flesh divided into joints like a sheep's,
Their backs straightened like a ram's;
Their flesh divided into joints like a colt's,
Their backs straightened like a greyhound's.
Their mouths opened wide as saws;
White foam mixed with blood
Scattered across their chests.
Their contracted hooves
Spread as wide as bowls;
The places where they trod
Were dug out like furnaces.
At a spur of the ending mountain,
At a sickle-shaped ridge and headland,
On the pass of Kara-Kapchal,
Toward the place where hero Khan Kongurbai's
Sentry lay,
Toward the branching successive ridges,
Facing forward and bracing his waist,
Your valiant Bakai now went,
To the projecting cliff and caravan road,
To the place where that ruined swine's
Fox lay.
Taking the lone path straight,
Your blessed uncle Bakai,
Holding it firmly by its collar,
Led Kumayyk.
Knowing many hidden turns of the land,
Your able saint Bakai—
When unlocking the land's secrets,
The ogre-like old man
Could not be confounded by villains.
When he traveled in darkness,
Once set on the trail, he never lost it.
Was Bakai not practiced
In learning land by reconnaissance?
Scouting and grieving over the land,
Was Bakai not practiced in it?
Onto a black rock large as a house,
Hero Bakai climbed;
He now turned Kökcholok's head.
While his gray wolf Manas lived,
What he had seen and learned
He now told the prince.
“My dear black-eyed one!
My spring flowing down the slope,
By the noble one gone to the next world,
My champion left as support!
Black-faced Beijing
Has a pass on which it relies,
And a place where it lies fortified.
That creature posted as its sentry—
At every moment, the swine
Has a khan who guards it!
It has a pass where it lies fortified,
And a place on which it relies.
It has a securely built stronghold,
And a fortified city
No mortal can destroy!
It has Kechil and its established order,
And people of forty tribes.
Gold comes from its land,
And it has countless kinds of wealth.
Here the infidels
Have a fox posted as sentinel.
There is the face of Kara-Kyya;
Here is the dark peril!
It is no pass to cross in sport;
Think upon it, my only one,
The Chinese are no easy people!
While bloodthirsty Manas lived,
While my champion Almambet was safe,
Syrgak, swift as a stray kid,
Was the companion
Of my precious elder Ala.
While my whole world, Almam, lived,
Yesterday, when he reconnoitered the road to Beijing,
Foremost among sixty,
The mightiest of the forty companions,
The champion boy Syrgak—
When he took him as companion,
When they scattered the Chinese herds,
And opened the road of the faith of Islam.
At the frontier lookout,
Here on this pass, its fox—
Yesterday, when Almam happened to shoot it,
Across the moon-yellow plain,
Pursuing it with Kökchebich,
When Syrgak reached and slew it,
When the champions caught the fox,
At the lookout farther on,
Champion lion Almam
Wrought slaughter there.
What use is telling or withholding it?
If told, the bastard's tale
Can never be exhausted.
There, at the spur of the ending mountain,
At the blunt projecting headland,
On the back of the black cliff,
Almam had dealt out grief.
On the guarded road no man trod,
A cub of the fox remained alive.
That orphan fox grew,
And became fat and vigorous, they say;
Its fire-red fur
Lengthened to forty fathoms.
This year, at the golden-poled tent,
For hero Kongurbai,
It has served faithfully, they say;
That fox now stands watch there, they say.
From seven days' journey away,
It knows a scent, I have heard.
The mighty Kalcha, hero Kongurbai,
Posted it firmly as a sentinel, they say,
And himself became khan of Beijing, they say!
If we let the fox suspect us,
Swifter than a flying bird,
It races across the plain
And in a moment gives word
To hero Khan Kongurbai.
No wind can match its running;
I hear it is a perfect fox,
One that raises alarm in Beijing,
The black eye of calamity, they say.
Asking what tradition says,
“This Kuutülkü standing here
Is the watchman himself, they say!
If we catch and do away with his fox,
It means God has granted him to us;
But if that bastard Kuutülkü
Escapes onto the open plain,
It means God has struck us down!
Here beside me is Kumayyk,
My beloved creature,
Encountered through the unseen,
Found by the favor of God.
When Bakai led the way,
In the desert of Median
A blue vulture bore him and left him.
They raised Kumayyk and made him a hound;
God Most High ordained it
And brought him to the Bloodthirsty One.
He was cherished more than a child;
While my mighty Manas lived,
My beloved Kumayyk
Was kept in a place of honor.
When Kumayyk had grown,
A tiger-skin covering
Was spread across his back,
And a collar of steel was placed around his neck!
When he stretched into his stride, he never rushed;
My beloved Kumayyk
Never retreated from a tiger.
When they loosed him on a bear and cried, ‘Attack!’
He mangled the place he bit,
